abstract: With the growth of increasingly complex devices, improving yield, quality, and manufacturing speed requires a new approach. Across 14 presentations and posters presented at SEMICON West 2026, Intel Foundry leaders and engineers shared research and emerging solutions for the AI-ready foundry of the future. By combining end-to-end metrology, intelligent analytics, and industry-wide standards, we can unlock scalable innovation for our customers. Semiconductor manufacturing is shifting from isolated optimization to connected intelligence, according to Intel Foundry’s Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor research and development, advanced packaging technology and manufacturing (APTM), in her keynote at the conference. Factory autonomy will not emerge from AI alone. It requires a system-first mindset based on a common foundation of trusted measurements, interoperable platforms, and advanced test infrastructure.¹ End-to-end metrology for proactive yield management For decades, metrology has served as a critical manufacturing checkpoint. Today, it is evolving into a control layer for proactive yield management. Modern semiconductor manufacturing demands more advanced metrology and defect control to address rising contamination risks, process sensitivities, and defectivity challenges. Hidden interactions among materials, equipment, chemicals, packaging polymers, and fab environments can undermine yield and often go undetected until late-stage manufacturing, increasing costs and slowing production. Rather than reacting to failures after they occur, semiconductor manufacturers like Intel Foundry are using predictive process control supported by continuous measurement and monitoring.² The requirement for end-to-end visibility does not stop at wafer fabrication. The…

abstract: Key Takeaways: AI accelerators and GPUs consume thousands of amperes at increasingly low voltages, causing a shift to vertical power delivery that brings regulation closer to loads. Advances in integrated voltage regulators and passive components are enabling new power architectures. Power delivery is becoming a system-level co-design challenge, expanding simulation needs and the role of OSATs. Power delivery is now a significant performance limiter in data center chips. The demands of AI and high-performance computing chips running near 0.7 V for a 600W GPU are forcing current to rise to 1,000 amps and beyond, compounding resistive losses and voltage droop across the PDN. Multi-chiplet constructions only compound these issues by further increasing current density and signal congestion. To solve these challenges, designers are turning to vertical power delivery networks, where the voltage regulator modules are relocated much closer to the processors from their position on the device periphery — to the PCB landside (under the PCB), inside the accelerator package, or inside the silicon interposer. Together with the growing customization of AI accelerator modules, there are many approaches on offer with varying design and manufacturing complexity. The vertical PDN trend began nearly a decade ago with the integration of backside power delivery networks (BPDNs) on the wafer backside, enabling fine-tuned power delivery more directly to the transistors while reducing IR drop across the tens of interconnect levels on-chip. That approach is being extended with increasingly sophisticated on-die decoupling capacitors (DCaps) formed in deep trenches as part of the BPDN. While this addresses high-frequency decoupling at the chip level, recent changes inside packages, interposers,…

summary.how: Survey of architectures: backside PDNs, on-die decoupling capacitors and integrated voltage regulators in packages and interposers.
summary.impact: Indirect relevance to electronics thermal management trends: higher current density and closer-in regulators raise local heat flux. No thermal analysis is stated in the excerpt.
summary.what: Article on vertical power delivery networks for AI accelerators, where voltage regulators move closer to the processor (under the PCB, in the package or in the interposer).
summary.why: Chips near 0.7 V at 600W draw about 1,000 A, and resistive losses and voltage droop make power delivery a performance limiter.

abstract: Key T ake a ways: CPO and NPO require new approaches for connecting optical fibers to chip packages. Detachable connectors can simplify assembly, test, and replacement of optical components. Numerous bespoke designs exist today, but standardization hasn’t begun yet. As photonics shifts from pluggable optical transceivers toward near- and co-packaged optics (NPO, CPO), engineers are devising new ways to attach fibers to the photonics chips on a board. Several different designs exist today, but so far there is no common interface. With pluggable photonics, lasers and connections are attached at the server faceplate, with the board itself housing only electronic components. Yet long electrical connections to the faceplate mean higher power and longer latency. Fibers would need to move onto the interior of the board to solve that. That eliminates the need for pluggables, but it requires new solutions. “With the rapid growth of generative AI, AI data centers are required to process enormous volumes of data faster and more efficiently than ever before,” said Yoshimasa Bando, principal scientist at Mitsubishi Chemical . “To meet this demand, further improvements in communication speed and energy efficiency have become critical challenges.” The goal of CPO and NPO is to reduce reliance on long electrical connections. Long lines One reason for maintaining faceplate pluggables is that lasers are not always reliable. Using a pluggable module makes it easy to replace the laser. “What we are focused on has the laser on the faceplate, because the laser is the highest reliability risk,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs . All connections, whether they have a laser or not, happen in pluggable modules today. That means the signals those fibers carry…

abstract: Key Takeaways: Agent orchestration at various stages of design, verification, and validation will require new methodologies and coordination across tools. Engineering expertise remains essential, and proprietary data is still siloed. Cost and complexity could limit adoption, giving larger companies an advantage. Experts at the Table : AI agents are moving into more parts of the chip design flow, but connecting them across different tools and processes remains a challenge. Questions also remain about how to capture decades of engineering expertise, protect proprietary design data, and keep costs manageable. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. I don’t get a sense that anybody really knows today how this combination is going to work. From what I have seen in different presentations, they’re still looking at how these things unfold. abstract: Key Takeaways: AI agents could make customized design workflows faster and less expensive to develop. Multi-agent systems introduce new challenges for orchestration, verification, and tool integration. Consumption-based pricing could reshape EDA business models, but trust and proprietary data remain obstacles. AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs. At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge. Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations. “We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents . “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in…

abstract: AI is driving the chip industry harder and faster than ever, requiring more decisions about everything from atomistic simulation to materials chemistry to the structural stability of a 3D architecture. The big question now is whether those decisions should be based on data or physics, or some combination of both. abstract: Documentation: https://alamode-code.github.io/alamode/ Packaging release; the calculations are unchanged. Build / packaging Binary wheels of the Python modules alm and anphon on PyPI for Linux (x86_64, aarch64) and macOS (arm64): pip install "alamode-python[openmpi]" (contributed by Hrushikesh Sahasrabuddhe, GitHub #338 ). The wheels contain neither the command-line programs and tool scripts nor the optional SuiteSparse solvers of alm. The Python distribution is named alamode-python (was alamode , a name that cannot be registered on PyPI). The modules are still imported as alm and anphon . If the Python package of 2.0.0 or 2.0.1 was installed from source, run pip uninstall alamode before installing this version. Boost >= 1.67 is required ( boost::sort::block_indirect_sort ); the build checks and the documentation said 1.66. The Python package requires Python >= 3.11 (was 3.9); it is built and tested with 3.11 and newer only. The Python build can leave out either module ( ALAMODE_PYTHON_ALM=OFF , ALAMODE_PYTHON_ANPHON=OFF ). License texts of the vendored code ( external/LICENSE_1_0.txt , external/niggli_LICENSE.txt ) and of the libraries bundled in the wheels ( python/LICENSES_bundled.txt ). Importing anphon without Open MPI says how to install it.

abstract: Researchers at Georgia Tech, NVIDIA Research , and Stanford University published “SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads.” Abstract Excerpt “Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20 μ s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even…

abstract: Tharunya Yogananda and Wantong Li of the University of California, Riverside published a technical paper titled “Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies.” Abstract Excerpt : “Recent generations of high bandwidth memory (HBM), such as HBM4, allow the base die of the memory stack to be manufactured using a logic process that can accommodate more complex controller functions next to the DRAM. We present the first systematic quantitative study of function-level controller placement between the host and the HBM4 base die on a silicon interposer. We divide the controller into its main functions and evaluate four placements, from a complete host controller to a complete base die controller, with intermediate placements that move maintenance or scheduling to the base die. “ Find the technical paper here . abstract: Researchers at Arizona State University and Ampere Computing published “DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration.” Abstract “Heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging enable chiplet-based system-on-chip (SoC) designs; however, they also introduce new yield challenges arising from manufacturing defects and complex die-to-die (D2D) interconnect constraints. In particular, lane-level defects, limited spares, and strict structural compatibility requirements impede the efficient assembly of functional systems from defective but repairable chiplets. We present DT-MATCH, a defect- and topology-aware chiplet matching framework that maximizes the number of functional SoCs under realistic assembly constraints. DT-MATCH provides two complementary approaches. The integer linear programming (ILP)-based approach is implemented using a batching strategy to approximate the exact formulation. The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.” Find the technical paper here . November 2026. abstract: We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road. One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method. How AMI works At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see. However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have. So, how do these defects typically present themselves? The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads.…

summary.how: A transducer sends ultrasound pulses, scanned across the sample; software analysis of the images supports accept or reject decisions.
summary.impact: Low relevance; packaging inspection, though delamination and thermal interface defects matter for thermal management industry context.
summary.what: An explainer of acoustic micro imaging (AMI), a high-frequency ultrasound inspection method for advanced packaging.
summary.why: Defects such as delaminations and air gaps cause electrical or mechanical failures and hurt yield and reliability as features shrink.
